newsitem.title: USA: Karadzic drops human rights case defense.
newsitem.headline: Karadzic drops human rights case defense.

text.p: Former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic will stop fighting a class action lawsuit brought here by victims of atrocities in Bosnia, plaintiffs' lawyers said on Tuesday.

The Centre for Constitutional Rights, which filed the suit on behalf of the victims, said that Karadzic's lawyer Ramsey Clark has told the court that his client will no longer mount a defence to the human rights lawsuit.

Jennie Green, a CCR lawyer, said the plaintiffs will ask the judge to issue a default judgment. She said the aim would be to go to trial so that the plaintiffs could establish a record against Karadzic by testifying about crimes against humanity.
She said they could also seek damages and that the CCR is pursuing information about Karadzic's assets.
The CCR said U.S. District Judge Peter Leisure forwarded a letter dated Feb. 28 from Clark, a former U.S. Attorney General, informing the court that Karadzic was dropping his defence.

"Dr. Karadzic advised me yesterday that he had decided it was impossible for him to defend these cases in the U.S. and he had instructed me ... I should take no further action in the trial court," Clark said in his letter.

In June, the U.S. Supreme Court denied an appeal by Karadzic's attorneys arguing the lawsuit should be dismissed because U.S. courts lacked jurisdiction and the case presented political questions inappropriate for judicial determination.
The ruling let stand a decision by the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in New York that reinstated the lawsuit filed in 1993 on behalf of the victims of the Bosnian civil war.

The appeals court ruled that Karadzic, president of the self-proclaimed Bosnian Serb Republic of Srpska, could be sued for the crimes against humanity both as an individual and in his capacity as a state politician.

The suit was filed under the Alien Tort Act enacted more than 200 years ago, which creates federal court jurisdiction for suits alleging civil wrongs committed anywhere in the world against non-Americans in violation of the law of nations.

The victims were Croat and Moslem citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, formerly part of the Republic of Yugoslavia. They alleged they and others suffered atrocities including murder, rape, forced prostitution, forced impregnation and torture carried out by a Bosnian Serb genocidal campaign conducted during the Bosnian civil war.

The lawsuit alleged that Karadzic, in his capacity as president, had authority over the military forces and that the injuries were part of a pattern of systematic human rights violations that he directed.
